opus-5.5.text:
I think robotics is finally at the point where the foundation model approach actually works, and that changes the economics of starting a company.

For a long time, robotics was a field where every application was its own bespoke engineering project. If you wanted a robot to pick up a particular kind of box in a particular warehouse, you'd spend years hand-tuning a system for exactly that task, and then it wouldn't generalize to the next one. That made it really hard to build a venture-scale business, because your costs scaled with every new customer.

What's different now is that we've learned, mostly from language models, that if you train large models on broad data, you get generalization almost for free. And people have started to show that the same recipe applies to robotics: you can take a vision-language model as a backbone, train it on diverse manipulation data, and get a policy that can do lots of tasks reasonably well, rather than one task perfectly. That's the shift from "programming" robots to "teaching" them.

The second thing is that the hardware has gotten dramatically cheaper. Arms and grippers that would have cost hundreds of thousands of dollars not that long ago are now in the range where a startup can buy a fleet and just collect data. And data is really the bottleneck. Unlike language, there's no internet of robot actions sitting there waiting to be scraped. So whoever figures out how to collect high-quality data at scale, whether through teleoperation, simulation, or learning from human video, has a real advantage, and that's a problem a new company can attack just as well as an incumbent.

And honestly, I think that's why it's a good moment for startups specifically. The big labs are focused on frontier language and reasoning models. Robotics requires a different kind of focus: physical operations, deployment, iterating with real customers. It's not obvious that the incumbents have a structural advantage there. So you have a window where the core technique is proven enough to bet on, but the field isn't locked up yet.

I'd add one caveat: I think it's still earlier than people sometimes hype it to be. We're maybe where language models were around GPT-2, where you can see it's going to work, but the reliability needed for real deployment, getting from 90% to 99.9%, is a long, hard road. The companies that win will be the ones that are patient about that, and that find the right early applications where imperfect performance is still valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says big labs are focused on frontier language and reasoning models, while robotics remains open to startups because incumbents lack a clear structural advantage.

r002.rationale: The response describes robotics as early and says reliable deployment is a long, hard road, but gives no prediction of commercialization within months to a few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's happened over the last couple of years is that the fundamental problem in robotics has changed. For a long time, the hard part wasn't the hardware, it was the intelligence. You could build a robot arm that was perfectly capable mechanically, but getting it to do anything in an unstructured environment required an enormous amount of hand-engineering, task by task, and it never generalized. We saw this at OpenAI with the robotics team: we could get a hand to solve a Rubik's Cube, but it took a staggering amount of simulation and effort for one task, and it didn't transfer to the next one.

What's changed is that foundation models have essentially solved a big chunk of the perception and reasoning problem for free. The model already knows what a cup is, what "put the dishes away" means, how to break a task into steps. So the thing you have to learn from scratch has shrunk down to the low-level control, the actual manipulation, and that's a much more tractable problem. You're no longer building the whole brain, you're building the last mile.

And that's exactly the kind of moment where new companies have an advantage. The incumbents in robotics are organized around the old world, where the moat was mechanical engineering and bespoke integration. The big AI labs mostly don't want to deal with hardware, because it's slow and it's messy and the iteration loops are terrible compared to just training a bigger language model. So there's this gap in the middle, where you need people who understand modern ML deeply and are also willing to grind through the physical-world problems, data collection, hardware reliability, all of it. That's a startup-shaped problem.

The other thing I'd say is that the data story is finally plausible. The reason language models worked is the internet existed. Robotics never had that. But now you have a few credible paths: teleoperation at scale, simulation that's good enough to transfer, and models that can learn from video of humans doing things. None of those are solved, but they're all real, and whoever figures out the data flywheel first has a shot at something that compounds the way the language models did. That's the bet. And if it works, the market isn't a narrow one, it's basically all of physical labor, which is a pretty compelling reason to go try.

r001.rationale: The response says big AI labs mostly avoid hardware and describes a gap for startups, but it does not say robotics is relatively far out on frontier AI labs’ roadmaps.

r002.rationale: The response gives no prediction that robotics will be commercialized in months to a few years.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics is attractive because there’s an opportunity to build something that wasn’t really possible before. Historically, you could make a robot do a specific task, but getting it to handle variation—different objects, different environments, unexpected situations—was incredibly difficult. You ended up doing a lot of engineering for each deployment.

The bet now is that AI can make more of that capability general. If you can teach a robot new tasks through data, rather than programming every behavior from scratch, the economics start to look very different.

For a new company, that creates an opening. You can pick a narrow application where the work is valuable, get robots into the real world, and learn from those deployments. You don’t have to solve all of robotics on day one. You need a useful starting point and a path for the system to improve as you scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes an opportunity for new robotics companies, but does not say robotics is relatively far out on frontier AI labs’ roadmaps.

r002.rationale: The response gives no prediction that robotics commercialization is months to a few years away.

sol-6.1.text:
I think robotics is attractive because we’re at a point where the intelligence is improving much faster than the hardware needs to. Historically, you had to build a very specialized system for a very specific task, and getting it to work reliably required an enormous amount of engineering. As models become more capable, you can start to imagine using the same underlying intelligence across a much broader range of tasks.

That creates an opening for new companies. You can pick a job that customers already spend a lot of money on, build a system that does that job well, and use what you learn from deployment to improve it. You don’t have to solve every problem in robotics on day one. You need to solve one valuable problem reliably, with economics that make sense.

r001.rationale: The response describes an opening for new robotics companies, but does not say robotics is relatively far out on frontier AI labs’ roadmaps.

r002.rationale: The response discusses improving models and building valuable systems, but gives no timeline of months to a few years for commercialization.
